claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 begins in a high-temperature BCC state.
The emergence of multiple phases is driven by kinetic competition between short-range atomic ordering and local compositional segregation.
Slower cooling provides sufficient time for diffusion-controlled atomic ordering.
Slower cooling provides sufficient time for elemental partitioning.
Diffusion-controlled ordering and elemental partitioning lead to secondary-phase nucleation from the high-temperature BCC state.
Short-range ordering and local compositional heterogeneities act as precursors to ordered secondary phases.
Slow cooling creates nanoscale regions with different local chemistries.
Nanoscale regions with different chemistries act as nucleation sites for secondary phases.
Rapid quenching locks in the high-temperature BCC structure.
Slowly cooled and subsequently thermally exposed samples will develop distinct secondary phases.
The predicted secondary phases or segregated structures will be observable by XRD and TEM.
Rapidly quenched and subsequently exposed samples will retain a predominantly metastable BCC phase with minimal phase segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies only when the cooling and aging treatments permit measurable atomic diffusion and ordering.
The proposed mechanism should not operate under extremely rapid cooling, such as melt-spinning, when atomic mobility is arrested.
No significant difference in phase composition or nanoscale ordering between slowly cooled and rapidly quenched samples would falsify the hypothesis.
